name: Privacy Regulation Theory
citation: Altman, I. (1975). The environment and social behavior. Brooks/Cole.

constructs.description: IC2 body-budget prediction + environmental predictability + IE-DPT activity frame configures interoceptive expectations.
Affordances + spatial enclosure + isovist control + environmental legibility enable boundary management.
Boundary violation + perceived control loss + interoceptive PE + allostatic demand. Density-is-not-crowding (Stokols) requires IE-DPT for explanation.
Social load deficit + DMN hyperengagement + dopaminergic deficit from lack of social stimulation.
Place recognition + hippocampal binding + learned safety signals establish spatial ownership.

irreducible_residual.narrative: The textbook IE-DPT bridge. Stokols' density-is-not-crowding finding is inexplicable without the explicit channel: the activity frame (IE-DPT) configures interoceptive expectations (IC), determining whether proximity generates positive or negative affective response. The open-plan office violates Privacy Regulation at multiple levels simultaneously.

function_form.function_form: S(p) = |D(p) − A(p)|; D(p) = desired privacy level; A(p) = achieved level

variables.D(p): Desired privacy level (varies with activity, personality, culture)
variables.A(p): Achieved privacy level in current environment

predictions: Privacy deficit (D > A) produces crowding stress; excess (A > D) produces isolation
Open-plan offices: 50% of workers report privacy deficit as top complaint

provenance.seminal_paper: Altman, I. (1975). The environment and social behavior: Privacy, personal space, territory, crowding. Monterey: Brooks/Cole Publishing Company.
provenance.conceptual_paper: Altman, I. (1976). Privacy: A conceptual analysis. Journal of Social Issues, 33(3), 7-28.
provenance.predecessor: Goffman's dramaturgical theory (impression management); territoriality research in animal behavior; environmental psychology tradition
provenance.historical_context: Irwin Altman developed privacy regulation theory as an overarching framework in environmental psychology. Core concept: privacy as selective control of access to self or one's group. Theory distinguishes privacy from loneliness and explains the dynamic optimization people perform to achieve desired privacy levels. Introduced the concept that successful privacy regulation requires multiple behavioral mechanisms: verbal communication, paraverbal behavior (tone, timing), non-verbal behavior (distance, posture, orientation), and environmental/spatial mechanisms (territoriality, personal space, enclosure). Later extended by Stokols (1972) with 'density is not crowding' distinction, recognizing IE-DPT dimension.
key_milestones: 1970s: Initial theoretical formulation in environmental psychology
1975: Comprehensive framework in The Environment and Social Behavior
1976: Conceptual analysis paper clarifying privacy as dynamic optimization
1980s-Present: Applications to residential design, workplace, healthcare, schools
2010s-Present: Modern workplace research (open-plan offices) validating theory
influenced_by: Irwin Altman (co-founder of environmental psychology field)
provenance.current_status: foundational framework widely applied in architecture, workplace design, and environmental psychology research
